P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which of the following is not a polynomial?

in a polynomial every power of the variable is a whole number (Topic 2). Why it applies: we only need to check the powers of x.

A root in a coefficient is allowed.
The variable is under a root.
Constants are polynomials (degree 0).
A fraction as a coefficient is allowed; the power 3 is a whole number.

Given: four expressions. Asked: the one that is not a polynomial.

Concept used: in a polynomial every power of the variable is a whole number (Topic 2). Why it applies: we only need to check the powers of x.

  1. 1

    (a) Powers of x are 2 and 1; 3\sqrt{3}3​ is only a coefficient — a polynomial.

  2. 2

    (b) x\sqrt{x}x​ is x to the power 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ — a fractional power, so not a polynomial.

  3. 3

    (c) A non-zero constant is a polynomial of degree 0.

  4. 4

    (d) x32=12x3\dfrac{x^3}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}x^32x3​=21​x3 — power 3 with coefficient 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ — a polynomial.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (b) ✔ The variable is under a root.
    • (a) ✘ A root in a coefficient is allowed.
    • (c) ✘ Constants are polynomials (degree 0).
    • (d) ✘ A fraction as a coefficient is allowed; the power 3 is a whole number.

  5. Check: write each as a sum of (number) × xnx^nxn: only (b) needs n=12n = \dfrac{1}{2}n=21​ ✔.

  6. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Rejecting (a) or (d) because of 3\sqrt{3}3​ or 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​. Only the powers of the variable matter.

standard form, then sum =−ba= -\dfrac{b}{a}=−ab​, product =ca= \dfrac{c}{a}=ac​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: the terms are written in the reverse order.

This is ba\dfrac{b}{a}ab​ — the minus sign of the sum is missing.
This reads a=3a = 3a=3 from the first term written; rearrange first.
The product ca\dfrac{c}{a}ac​ has no minus sign.

Given: p(x)=3−5x+2x2p(x) = 3 - 5x + 2x^2p(x)=3−5x+2x2. Asked: sum and product of zeroes.

Concept used: standard form, then sum =−ba= -\dfrac{b}{a}=−ab​, product =ca= \dfrac{c}{a}=ac​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: the terms are written in the reverse order.

  1. 1

    Standard form: 2x2−5x+32x^2 - 5x + 32x2−5x+3, so a=2a = 2a=2, b=−5b = -5b=−5, c=3c = 3c=3.

  2. 2

    Sum.

    −ba=−−52=52-\dfrac{b}{a} = -\dfrac{-5}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2}−ab​=−2−5​=25​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    ca=32\dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{3}{2}ac​=23​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    • (d) ✘ The product ca\dfrac{c}{a}ac​ has no minus sign.

  4. Check: 2x2−5x+3=(2x−3)(x−1)2x^2 - 5x + 3 = (2x - 3)(x - 1)2x2−5x+3=(2x−3)(x−1), zeroes 32\dfrac{3}{2}23​ and 1: sum 52\dfrac{5}{2}25​ ✔, product 32\dfrac{3}{2}23​ ✔.

    Common trap: Reading a, b, c in the order the terms are written.

Given: p(x)=4x2+8x+3p(x) = 4x^2 + 8x + 3p(x)=4x2+8x+3. Asked: is p(−12)=0p\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0p(−21​)=0?

  1. 1

    Substitute x=−12x = -\dfrac{1}{2}x=−21​.

    p(−12)=4×14+8×(−12)+3p\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{4} + 8 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 3p(−21​)=4×41​+8×(−21​)+3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Simplify.

    =1−4+3=0= 1 - 4 + 3 = 0=1−4+3=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    p(−12)=0p\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0p(−21​)=0, so −12-\dfrac{1}{2}−21​ is a zero.

  4. Check: 4x2+8x+3=(2x+1)(2x+3)4x^2 + 8x + 3 = (2x + 1)(2x + 3)4x2+8x+3=(2x+1)(2x+3); the factor 2x+12x + 12x+1 is 0 at x=−12x = -\dfrac{1}{2}x=−21​ ✔.

P4● FoundationShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Find the zeroes of 3x+2x2−93x + 2x^2 - 93x+2x2−9 and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.

Full solution

Given: p(x)=3x+2x2−9p(x) = 3x + 2x^2 - 9p(x)=3x+2x2−9. Asked: the zeroes; verify.

Concept used: standard form, split the middle term, then the relationships (Topic 4). Why it applies: the terms are out of order.

  1. 1

    Standard form.

    2x2+3x−9,a=2,  b=3,  c=−92x^2 + 3x - 9, \qquad a = 2, \; b = 3, \; c = -92x2+3x−9,a=2,b=3,c=−9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Product ac=−18ac = -18ac=−18, sum 333: the pair is 666 and −3-3−3.

    2x2+6x−3x−92x^2 + 6x - 3x - 92x2+6x−3x−9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Group.

    2x(x+3)−3(x+3)2x(x + 3) - 3(x + 3)2x(x+3)−3(x+3)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Take out (x+3)(x + 3)(x+3).

    (2x−3)(x+3)(2x - 3)(x + 3)(2x−3)(x+3)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Zeroes: x=32x = \dfrac{3}{2}x=23​ and x=−3x = -3x=−3.

  6. 6

    Sum.

    32+(−3)=−32,−ba=−32\dfrac{3}{2} + (-3) = -\dfrac{3}{2}, \qquad -\dfrac{b}{a} = -\dfrac{3}{2}23​+(−3)=−23​,−ab​=−23​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Product.

    32×(−3)=−92,ca=−92\dfrac{3}{2} \times (-3) = -\dfrac{9}{2}, \qquad \dfrac{c}{a} = -\dfrac{9}{2}23​×(−3)=−29​,ac​=−29​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Verified.

  9. Check: p(−3)=−9+18−9=0p(-3) = -9 + 18 - 9 = 0p(−3)=−9+18−9=0 ✔.

  10. Answer Zeroes 32\dfrac{3}{2}23​ and −3-3−3; sum −32-\dfrac{3}{2}−23​, product −92-\dfrac{9}{2}−29​ ✔

    Common trap: Taking a=3a = 3a=3 (the first coefficient written). Then −ba-\dfrac{b}{a}−ab​ and ca\dfrac{c}{a}ac​ come out wrong and the "verification" fails.

P5● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

The graph of y=p(x)y = p(x)y=p(x) crosses the x-axis at x=−3x = -3x=−3, touches it at x=1x = 1x=1, and crosses it again at x=4x = 4x=4. It crosses the y-axis at y=6y = 6y=6. The number of zeroes of p(x)p(x)p(x) is:

count points on the x-axis; a touch counts once (Topic 3). Why it applies: each point where the graph meets the x-axis is one zero.

Leaves out the touching point.
Counts the touch twice, or counts the y-axis point as a zero.
Makes both of those mistakes.

Given: two crossings and one touch on the x-axis; a y-intercept of 6. Asked: the number of zeroes.

Concept used: count points on the x-axis; a touch counts once (Topic 3). Why it applies: each point where the graph meets the x-axis is one zero.

  1. 1

    Points on the x-axis: −3-3−3 (cross), 111 (touch), 444 (cross).

  2. 2

    That is 3 points, so 3 zeroes.

  3. 3

    The y-intercept 666 is p(0)p(0)p(0); it is not a zero.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (b) ✔
    • (a) ✘ Leaves out the touching point.
    • (c) ✘ Counts the touch twice, or counts the y-axis point as a zero.
    • (d) ✘ Makes both of those mistakes.

  4. Check: a polynomial such as −12(x+3)(x−1)2(x−4)-\dfrac{1}{2}(x + 3)(x - 1)^2(x - 4)−21​(x+3)(x−1)2(x−4) has exactly this picture: zeroes −3-3−3, 111 (touch) and 444, and p(0)=6p(0) = 6p(0)=6 — three points on the x-axis ✔.

  5. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Counting a touching point as two zeroes.
P6● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A parabola cuts the x-axis at (−1,0)(-1, 0)(−1,0) and (3,0)(3, 0)(3,0), and the y-axis at (0,−3)(0, -3)(0,−3). Which of these is a zero of the polynomial?

zeroes are the x-coordinates of the points on the x-axis (Topic 3). Why it applies: only (−1,0)(-1, 0)(−1,0) and (3,0)(3, 0)(3,0) are on the x-axis.

−3-3−3 is where the graph meets the y-axis: it is p(0)p(0)p(0).
x=0x = 0x=0 is where the graph meets the y-axis; there p(0)=−3≠0p(0) = -3 \neq 0p(0)=−3=0.
1 is halfway between the zeroes (the x-coordinate of the lowest point), not a zero.

Given: the three points where the parabola meets the axes. Asked: a zero.

Concept used: zeroes are the x-coordinates of the points on the x-axis (Topic 3). Why it applies: only (−1,0)(-1, 0)(−1,0) and (3,0)(3, 0)(3,0) are on the x-axis.

  1. 1

    Points on the x-axis: (−1,0)(-1, 0)(−1,0) and (3,0)(3, 0)(3,0).

  2. 2

    Zeroes: −1-1−1 and 333. Of the options, only 3 is a zero.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (b) ✔
    • (a) ✘ −3-3−3 is where the graph meets the y-axis: it is p(0)p(0)p(0).
    • (c) ✘ x=0x = 0x=0 is where the graph meets the y-axis; there p(0)=−3≠0p(0) = -3 \neq 0p(0)=−3=0.
    • (d) ✘ 1 is halfway between the zeroes (the x-coordinate of the lowest point), not a zero.

  3. Check: the polynomial is (x+1)(x−3)=x2−2x−3(x + 1)(x - 3) = x^2 - 2x - 3(x+1)(x−3)=x2−2x−3; p(3)=0p(3) = 0p(3)=0 ✔ and p(0)=−3p(0) = -3p(0)=−3 ✔.

  4. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Choosing the y-intercept.

    Product.

    32×32=34,ca=34\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{3}{4}, \qquad \dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{3}{4}23​​×23​​=43​,ac​=43​Swipe to see the whole equation →

P27●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: the school gate

The entrance gate of a school has a parabolic arch. Taking the ground as the x-axis and measuring in metres, the arch follows the curve y=−x2+8x−12y = -x^2 + 8x - 12y=−x2+8x−12, where y is the height above the ground.

(a) Does the arch open upwards or downwards? Give a reason. (1)
(b) At which two points does the arch meet the ground? How wide is the arch at ground level? (1)
(c) Verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients of −x2+8x−12-x^2 + 8x - 12−x2+8x−12. (2)

OR
(c) The highest point of the arch is directly above the midpoint of the two points in (b). Find the height of the arch. (2)

Full solution

Given: p(x)=−x2+8x−12p(x) = -x^2 + 8x - 12p(x)=−x2+8x−12. Asked: parts (a)–(c).

Concept used: sign of a (Topic 3); zeroes by factorising and verification (Topic 4). Why it applies: the ground is the x-axis, so the feet of the arch are the zeroes.

  1. 1

    (a)

    a=−1<0a = -1 < 0a=−1<0, so the parabola opens downwards (an arch shape).

  2. 2

    (b)

    Factorise.

    −x2+8x−12=−(x2−8x+12)=−(x−2)(x−6)-x^2 + 8x - 12 = -(x^2 - 8x + 12) = -(x - 2)(x - 6)−x2+8x−12=−(x2−8x+12)=−(x−2)(x−6)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Zeroes: 2 and 6. The arch meets the ground at x=2x = 2x=2 and x=6x = 6x=6; width 6−2=46 - 2 = 46−2=4 m.

  4. 4

    (c)

    Sum 2+6=82 + 6 = 82+6=8; −ba=−8−1=8-\dfrac{b}{a} = -\dfrac{8}{-1} = 8−ab​=−−18​=8 ✔. Product 2×6=122 \times 6 = 122×6=12; ca=−12−1=12\dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{-12}{-1} = 12ac​=−1−12​=12 ✔. Verified.

  5. 5

    (c) OR

    Midpoint of 2 and 6 is 4. Height:

    y=−16+32−12=4 my = -16 + 32 - 12 = 4 \text{ m}y=−16+32−12=4 mSwipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: p(2)=−4+16−12=0p(2) = -4 + 16 - 12 = 0p(2)=−4+16−12=0 ✔ and p(6)=−36+48−12=0p(6) = -36 + 48 - 12 = 0p(6)=−36+48−12=0 ✔.

  7. Answer (a) downwards, since a=−1<0a = -1 < 0a=−1<0 (b) at x=2x = 2x=2 m and x=6x = 6x=6 m; width 4 m (c) sum 8=−ba8 = -\dfrac{b}{a}8=−ab​, product 12=ca12 = \dfrac{c}{a}12=ac​ (c OR) 4 m

    Common trap: In (c), using b=8b = 8b=8 and a=1a = 1a=1 (ignoring the minus on x2x^2x2): the product would come out as −12-12−12.

P29●●● AdvancedTrue/False with justification · 2 marksOriginal

True or false? Justify. "If the graph of a polynomial meets the x-axis at exactly two points, the polynomial must be quadratic."

Full solution

Given: a statement about graphs. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: a polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes — but it can have fewer (Topic 3). Why it applies: a cubic or higher polynomial may meet the axis at only two points.

  1. 1

    To show the statement is false, one counter-example is enough.

  2. 2

    Take the cubic x3−4x2+4x=x(x−2)2x^3 - 4x^2 + 4x = x(x - 2)^2x3−4x2+4x=x(x−2)2. Its graph crosses the x-axis at 0 and touches it at 2.

  3. 3

    That is exactly two points, yet the polynomial has degree 3.

  4. Check: p(0)=0p(0) = 0p(0)=0 and p(2)=8−16+8=0p(2) = 8 - 16 + 8 = 0p(2)=8−16+8=0, and x(x−2)2x(x - 2)^2x(x−2)2 has no other zero ✔.

  5. Answer False. For example, the cubic x(x−2)2x(x - 2)^2x(x−2)2 meets the x-axis at exactly two points.

    Common trap: Reversing the rule. "A quadratic meets the axis at most twice" does not mean "meeting it twice makes it quadratic".

E6● FoundationMCQ · 1 markNCERT Exemplar Ch 2, Ex 2.1 Q11

Which of the following is not the graph of a quadratic polynomial?
(Graphs described in words.)

a quadratic's graph is a parabola, with one turning point and at most 2 zeroes (Topic 3). Why it applies: (D) has two turning points and three zeroes.

, (B), (C) are parabolas (one turn), opening up or down.
turns twice and meets the x-axis three times; a quadratic has at most 2 zeroes. So (D) is not a quadratic (it looks like a cubic).

Given: four graphs. Asked: the one that cannot be a quadratic.

Concept used: a quadratic's graph is a parabola, with one turning point and at most 2 zeroes (Topic 3). Why it applies: (D) has two turning points and three zeroes.

  1. 1

    (A), (B), (C) are parabolas (one turn), opening up or down.

  2. 2

    (D) turns twice and meets the x-axis three times; a quadratic has at most 2 zeroes. So (D) is not a quadratic (it looks like a cubic).

    Reasoning for each option: (D) ✔. (A) ✘ a parabola with no zeroes is still quadratic. (B) ✘ a touching parabola is quadratic (equal zeroes). (C) ✘ a downward parabola is quadratic.

  3. Check: three zeroes would need degree at least 3 ✔.

  4. Answer (D)

    Common trap: Choosing (A) because it has no zeroes. Having no zeroes does not stop a polynomial being quadratic.

Is the following statement 'True' or 'False'? Justify your answer. If the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial ax2+bx+cax^2 + bx + cax2+bx+c are both positive, then a, b and c all have the same sign.

Full solution

Given: both zeroes positive. Asked: true or false.

Concept used: sum −ba-\dfrac{b}{a}−ab​, product ca\dfrac{c}{a}ac​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: positive zeroes force the signs of these ratios.

    Sum >0> 0>0: −ba>0-\dfrac{b}{a} > 0−ab​>0, so ba<0\dfrac{b}{a} < 0ab​<0 — b and a have opposite signs.

  2. 2

    So a, b and c cannot all have the same sign.

    Common trap: Remembering the companion fact ("both negative ⇒ same sign", which is true) and applying it here.

E9 (Exemplar Ex 2.2, Q2 (ii))●● StandardTrue/False with justification · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 2, Ex 2.2 Q2 (ii)

Is the following statement 'True' or 'False'? Justify your answer. If the graph of a polynomial intersects the x-axis at only one point, it cannot be a quadratic polynomial.

Full solution

Given: a graph meeting the x-axis at one point. Asked: can it be quadratic?

Concept used: case (ii) of the parabola — a touch (Topic 3). Why it applies: a parabola can meet the axis at exactly one point.

  1. 1

    The graph of x2−2x+1=(x−1)2x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2x2−2x+1=(x−1)2 touches the x-axis at (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0) only.

  2. 2

    It is a quadratic. So the statement is false.

  3. Check: (x−1)2=0(x - 1)^2 = 0(x−1)2=0 only when x=1x = 1x=1 ✔.

  4. Answer False. For example, x2−2x+1x^2 - 2x + 1x2−2x+1 meets the x-axis only at x=1x = 1x=1.

    Common trap: Thinking "one point ⇒ linear". A parabola that touches also meets the axis at one point.

The below picture are few natural examples of parabolic shape which is represented by a quadratic polynomial. A parabolic arch is an arch in the shape of a parabola. In structures, their curve represents an efficient method of load, and so can be found in bridges and in architecture in a variety of forms.

(Pictures: an arched stone gateway and a suspension bridge.)

  1. In the standard form of quadratic polynomial, ax2+bx+cax^2 + bx + cax2+bx+c, a, b and c are (a) All are real numbers. (b) All are rational numbers. (c) 'a' is a non zero real number and b and c are any real numbers. (d) All are integers.

  4. The graph of x2+1=0x^2 + 1 = 0x2+1=0 (a) Intersects x-axis at two distinct points. (b) Touches x-axis at a point. (c) Neither touches nor intersects x-axis. (d) Either touches or intersects x-axis.

If the sum of the roots is −p-p−p and product of the roots is −1p-\dfrac{1}{p}−p1​, then the quadratic polynomial is (a) k(−px2+xp+1)k\left(-px^2 + \dfrac{x}{p} + 1\right)k(−px2+px​+1) (b) k(px2−xp−1)k\left(px^2 - \dfrac{x}{p} - 1\right)k(px2−px​−1) (c) k(x2+px−1p)k\left(x^2 + px - \dfrac{1}{p}\right)k(x2+px−p1​) (d) k(x2−px+1p)k\left(x^2 - px + \dfrac{1}{p}\right)k(x2−px+p1​)

Full solution

Given: five questions on the standard form, equal zeroes, reciprocal zeroes, a graph and building a polynomial. Asked: five answers.

Concept used: a≠0a \neq 0a=0 (Topic 2); a touching parabola (Topic 3); product =1= 1=1 for reciprocals and k{x2−Sx+P}k\{x^2 - Sx + P\}k{x2−Sx+P} (Topic 5).

    a must be non-zero (or it is not quadratic); b and c can be any real numbers → (c).

  2. 2

C3 — Case: the path of a ball●● StandardCase/source-based · 5 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Polynomials, Case Study 3

Basketball and soccer are played with a spherical ball. Even though an athlete dribbles the ball in both sports, a basketball player uses his hands and a soccer player uses his feet. Usually, soccer is played outdoors on a large field and basketball is played indoor on a court made out of wood. The projectile (path traced) of soccer ball and basketball are in the form of parabola representing quadratic polynomial.

(Pictures: the arc of a basketball shot and of a football free kick.)

  1. The shape of the path traced shown is (a) Spiral (b) Ellipse (c) Linear (d) Parabola
  2. The graph of parabola opens upwards, if _______ (a) a=0a = 0a=0 (b) a<0a < 0a<0 (c) a>0a > 0a>0 (d) a≥0a \geq 0a≥0
  3. Observe the following graph and answer. In the above graph, how many zeroes are there for the polynomial? (Graph described: a curve rising from the lower left, crossing the x-axis at −3-3−3, peaking near (−2,4)(-2, 4)(−2,4), crossing at −1-1−1, dipping to about (0.8,−8)(0.8, -8)(0.8,−8) after crossing the y-axis at −6-6−6, and rising to cross at 2.) (a) 0 (b) 1 (c) 2 (d) 3
  4. The three zeroes in the above shown graph are (b) 2, 3, −1 (c) −2, 3, 1 (d) −3, −1, 2 (e) −2, −3, −1
  5. What will be the expression of the polynomial? (a) x3+2x2−5x−6x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6x3+2x2−5x−6 (b) x3+2x2−5x+6x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x + 6x3+2x2−5x+6 (c) x3+2x2+5x−6x^3 + 2x^2 + 5x - 6x3+2x2+5x−6 (d) x3+2x2+5x+6x^3 + 2x^2 + 5x + 6x3+2x2+5x+6

Full solution

Given: five questions. Asked: five answers.

Concept used: parabola and sign of a; counting and reading zeroes (Topic 3); building a polynomial from its zeroes (Topic 5).

  1. 1

    (d) parabola.

  2. 2

    Opens upwards when a>0a > 0a>0 → (c).

  3. 3

    Three crossing points → (d).

  4. 4

    The crossings are at −3-3−3, −1-1−1 and 222 — the option printed with the label (d).

  5. 5

    A polynomial with zeroes −3-3−3, −1-1−1, 2 is (x+3)(x+1)(x−2)=(x2+4x+3)(x−2)=x3+2x2−5x−6(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2) = (x^2 + 4x + 3)(x - 2) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6(x+3)(x+1)(x−2)=(x2+4x+3)(x−2)=x3+2x2−5x−6 → (a).

  6. Answer 1 (d) · 2 (c) · 3 (d) · 4 the option "−3, −1, 2" · 5 (a)

    Note on part 4: the bank prints the options with the labels (b), (c), (d), (e) — there is no (a) — and its key says "c) −3, −1, 2", although "−3, −1, 2" is printed against (d). The intended answer is clearly −3, −1, 2.

    Note on parts 3–5: the graph here is a cubic (degree 3), not a parabola, even though the case is about parabolas. Part 5 builds a cubic from its zeroes by multiplying (x−α)(x−β)(x−γ)(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)(x - \gamma)(x−α)(x−β)(x−γ) — the same idea as k(x−α)(x−β)k(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)k(x−α)(x−β) in Topic 5.

  7. Check: the cubic's y-intercept is −6-6−6 ✔, matching the graph.

    Common trap: Choosing (b) in part 5, which has constant +6+6+6; the graph crosses the y-axis below the origin.
